name: High-effort / low-effort post tags

lead: On forums such as looksmax.org, thread titles are often prefixed with '[High effort]' or 'high effort'. The tag tells readers the author spent time researching and writing a detailed guide, for example on physique, skincare, photos or pharmacology. A matching 'no value post' prefix is used for short, casual threads that the author does not expect to contain useful information.

For people trying to improve their appearance, the tags work as a rough filter. Long guides on topics such as upper-body training, grooming or dating-profile photos are easier to find when marked, and casual updates are labelled so they do not get mistaken for advice. The tags are applied by the posters themselves.

paras: A poster types the tag at the start of a thread title, then writes a long structured post, often with sections and a conclusion. Readers search for or scroll for the tag to find guides. Casual posts use 'no value post' in the same position, often as a self-deprecating joke.

Because anyone can add the tag, it describes the author's effort rather than the correctness of the content. Several tagged threads cover medical or pharmacological topics, and readers rely on the usual caution about forum health information.

angle.text: The tags do not change appearance themselves. They steer readers toward long, structured guides on looks topics such as physique, skin, grooming and photos, and mark casual chatter as such, which shortens the search for detailed material.

lead: High-effort and low-effort post tags are informal title prefixes used on looksmaxxing forums, most visibly looksmax.org. A thread starting with 'high effort' (or '[High effort]') announces a long, researched or carefully structured write-up, while a thread starting with 'no value post' announces a short or casual contribution that the author does not expect anyone to learn from.[1][2][3]

For people trying to improve how they look, the tags work as a signpost. Tagged threads on the forum cover physique development, dating-profile photos, softmaxxing and grooming, makeup and temporary 'fraud' methods for events, skin and mole removal, and fitness styles, each presented as a comprehensive guide.[4][5][6][7][8][9] Readers who want detailed material can look for the tag, while personal updates and jokes are labelled so they are not mistaken for advice.[3][10]

The convention belongs to a wider internet tradition. The slang term 'effortpost' is defined by Wiktionary as a thoughtful, useful post, the opposite of a 'shitpost', and the word 'shitpost' itself has been traced to Something Awful forum threads in 2007.[11][12] Looksmaxxing forums adopted their own wording, in which effort and value are announced by the poster in the title.[1][3]

The tags are a community habit, not a software feature, and no published study has examined them. Academic work on effort, such as the effort-reward imbalance model in occupational health and the learned-industriousness theory in psychology, deals with effort in general and not with forum labels.[13][14]
infobox: high effort, [High effort], no value post
Signal the length and effort of a post

paras: A 'high effort' tag is typed into the thread title by the author, usually at the start and sometimes in square brackets. On looksmax.org, titles using it include a 'full pill spectrum' write-up on black-pill and blue-pill beliefs, a guide to building an upper body, a dating-app pictures guide, a 'prettyboymaxxing' softmaxxing guide, a fitness-styles tier list, a guide to moles and their removal, a multi-part guide to makeup, bloat reduction and height-and-frame 'frauds' for occasions, a ranking of money methods, and a photo-morph of a celebrity.[1][2][4][5][6][7][8][9]

Several of the threads add other community labels beside the tag, such as 'megaguide', 'guide' or audience markers aimed at younger members, which tells readers the intended scope and audience of the post as well as its effort level.[5][8][9] Some tagged threads cover medicines or compounds that members discuss in connection with puberty and appearance; the tag in these cases describes how long and detailed the author's post is, and says nothing about its safety or accuracy.[15]

The counterpart 'no value post' is used for brief personal updates: a note about a supplement that arrived by mail, a remark that mewing made the poster's tongue strong, a story about almost getting a phone number, or a dating setback described by the poster.[3][10][16][17] Authors use it as a modest disclaimer, in the same position in the title as the high-effort tag.

The wider vocabulary has older roots. Know Your Meme traces the earliest known use of 'shitposting' to April 2007 on the Something Awful forums, where a user used it for worthless threads, and notes the 4chan FAQ definition of knowingly contributing low-quality or off-topic posts.[12] Wiktionary lists 'effortpost' (also written 'effort post') as the corresponding term for a constructive, meaningful post, with a verb form 'effortposting'; it does not date the word.[11]

Looksmaxxing itself, according to Wikipedia, grew out of online communities of the 2010s, including the now-defunct PSL forums, before spreading to TikTok in the early 2020s and attracting press coverage from 2023.[18] looksmax.org does not appear in that article, and no source documents when the specific 'high effort' and 'no value post' prefixes first appeared there. The earliest-numbered 'no value post' threads on the forum carry very low thread numbers, which indicates the label was in use from the site's early period.[3][10][16][17]

Members treat the high-effort tag as a promise that the poster compiled information, often with sections, summaries and a conclusion. Authors frame their guides as time-saving collections, for example in a thread that lists a table of contents and says the guide will cover makeup, bloat reduction and height-and-frame methods meant for occasions such as a date.[2] Replies commonly acknowledge the work, for instance with a short remark that the thread is useful.[2]

Because the label is self-applied, it signals intent rather than accuracy. Forum guides on medical, hormonal or pharmacological topics carry the same tag as guides on photography or posture, and the forum's own culture of replies, corrections and quote-threads is the usual place where readers cross-check claims.[4][6][15]

No studies found. Related academic work on effort and reward includes a review of the effort-reward imbalance model in occupational health psychology and a psychology paper on learned industriousness, neither of which concerns forum tags.[13][14]

lore.intro: Members describe the tag as a way to separate worked-out guides from casual chatter, while treating the label itself as the poster's own claim.[1][2][3]

Looksmaxxing forums such as the PSL sites develop out of incel and manosphere communities.[18]
Looksmaxxing spreads to TikTok, widening the audience for forum guides.[18]
Business Insider (8 Nov) and The New York Times (6 Nov) cover the looksmaxxing trend.[18]
